title: Monsoon in the hills: is July worth it, and where to go
meta_description: Is July a good time for Darjeeling and the Dooars? Rain, landslides, closed parks, cheap rooms, tea gardens and the places that still work in the monsoon.
summary: July is the wettest month in the Darjeeling hills and the Dooars parks are closed, so it is not for mountain views or safaris. It is worth it for green tea gardens, empty towns, cool air and room rates 20–40 percent lower. Base yourself in Darjeeling, Kurseong or Mirik, keep plans short and check roads daily.
key_takeaways: July brings the heaviest rain of the year to Darjeeling, with mist most days and Kanchenjunga hidden for weeks at a time.
Jaldapara, Gorumara and Singalila National Park are closed for the monsoon, usually from mid-June to mid-September.
Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik and the tea gardens stay open, quiet and green, and many hotels offer off-season discounts.
Landslides close hill roads and toy train sections often, so travel by day, keep spare time and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: What July is really like
paras: The south-west monsoon usually reaches the Darjeeling hills in the first half of June and stays until late September. July is its heart. Darjeeling town gets roughly 600 to 800 mm of rain in the month in a typical year, more than it gets in the whole of winter, and the hills further down towards Kurseong and the Dooars below are wetter still. Rain does not fall all day every day. A common pattern is a soft drizzle at dawn, a dry spell in the morning, heavy showers in the afternoon and steady rain at night.

Mist is the other constant. Cloud sits in the valleys and drifts up through the town, so that the far side of a tea garden comes and goes in minutes. Daytime temperatures in Darjeeling are comfortable, about 15 to 20 °C, and it never gets truly cold. What you will almost never see is Kanchenjunga. On a handful of July mornings the cloud breaks for an hour; most visitors in this month go home without a mountain photograph.

So the honest answer is that July is not the month for views, treks or safaris. It is a good month for a quiet, cheap, green trip if you like rain, tea and walking under an umbrella, and if you build your plans around the weather instead of fighting it.

sections.heading: What is closed or risky
paras: Some things are simply off the table. Jaldapara and Gorumara, along with the other Dooars parks, close for the monsoon, usually from 16 June to 15 September. Singalila National Park, and with it the Sandakphu trek, closes in the same window. Long walks on forest trails bring leeches, which are harmless but unpleasant, and slippery stone paths.

Roads are the real risk. Landslides are common on the routes up from Siliguri, especially Rohini Road and the Pankhabari road to Kurseong, the Hill Cart Road beside the toy train line, and NH10 along the Teesta, which has had repeated closures since the 2023 flood. A slide can close a road for an hour or several days. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway often suspends or shortens its long-distance services from New Jalpaiguri in the monsoon when the line is blocked, though the short joy rides between Darjeeling and Ghoom usually keep running. Check current status before you travel.
list: Travel up and down the hills only in daylight, ideally before noon.
Ask your driver which road is open that morning; they hear first.
Keep a spare day before any train or flight home.
Skip North Sikkim, Sandakphu and long forest treks in July.

sections.heading: Where to go instead
paras: The places that work best in July have three things in common: they are on reliable roads, they have things to do indoors or close by, and they look their best wet. The table sums up our view.

Mirik is the easiest of these from the plains, about 50 km from Siliguri on a road that usually holds up well, and its lake walk and tea slopes are a pleasant half day even in light rain. Lamahatta and Takdah, on the road between Darjeeling and Kalimpong, are for people who want to sit with a book in a homestay and watch cloud move through pine forest; go only when the road is reported open.

sections.heading: Darjeeling on a wet day
paras: Darjeeling is built for rain. The Himalayan Mountaineering Institute and its museum, with Tenzing Norgay's story and the gear of early Everest expeditions, sit inside the same campus as the Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park, where red pandas and snow leopards are easier to see on cool, misty days; both are usually closed on Thursdays. The Bhutia Busty and Ghoom monasteries, the Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre and the old churches make good short outings between showers.

Then there is the eating. A plate of hot momos at a Tibetan kitchen below Chowrasta, a pot of tea at a tea room on the Mall, or a long breakfast at Keventer's or Glenary's feel very different with rain on the window. We plan July days in Darjeeling as one outing in the morning, a long lunch, and a walk on the Mall in the evening when the clouds lift.

sections.heading: Tea gardens in the monsoon
paras: July is the busiest month of the year in the gardens. The monsoon flush, the third harvest after the spring first flush and the early summer second flush, brings fast growth and heavy plucking. Women pluckers move along the rows with baskets on their backs from early morning, and factories run long hours. Monsoon tea is stronger and darker, and most of it goes into blends, so it is cheap to buy and good with milk.

Kurseong is the place to see this. Makaibari, one of the oldest gardens in the hills, has village homestays where families who work in the garden host guests, and you can walk the rows and visit the factory. Around Mirik and on the Rohini side the gardens fall steeply away under the cloud, and a walk through them on a dry morning is one of the most beautiful things the monsoon offers.

sections.heading: The Dooars in July
paras: With the parks shut, the Dooars are not a July destination for most people. It is hot and very humid, with afternoon temperatures above 30 °C, heavy downpours, and rivers that rise fast. The Murti, Jaldhaka and other rivers can swell within an hour after rain in the hills, so riverside picnics and wading are a bad idea in this season.

That said, if you are passing through Siliguri on the way to the hills, a drive through the tea gardens of the Dooars is green and striking, and the forest edges at Lataguri and Murti are lush. Some lodges stay open at low rates. Treat it as a short stop rather than the point of the trip, and come back between October and May for the wildlife.

sections.heading: Money, packing and our verdict
paras: Rooms are where July saves you money. Outside the Bengali and national holidays, many Darjeeling and Kurseong hotels and homestays drop rates by 20 to 40 percent, and walk-in bargaining works. Reserved cars are easier to find, and the town's restaurants and lanes are relaxed. Pack a good umbrella, a light rain jacket, quick-dry clothes, shoes with grip that you do not mind getting wet, and a few plastic bags for electronics. Salt or a little soap helps with leeches if you walk forest paths.

Is July worth it? For views, treks and safaris, no; come between October and May. For a slow, cool, cheap few days of tea, mist, food and long conversations with hosts who have time to talk, yes, as long as you stay in the towns, travel by day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is July a good time to visit Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Only if you want a quiet, green and cheap trip. July is the wettest month, mist hides Kanchenjunga most days and landslides can close roads. In return, the town is uncrowded, tea gardens are at their greenest and many rooms are 20–40 percent cheaper. Stay in Darjeeling, Kurseong or Mirik, travel by day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are Jaldapara and Gorumara open in July?
faqs.a: No. The Dooars national parks, including Jaldapara and Gorumara, usually close for the monsoon from 16 June to 15 September for animal breeding and because forest roads become impassable. Safaris resume in mid-September, with the best sightings from late February to May. Check current status before you travel, as dates are set each year by the forest department.

faqs.q: Does the toy train run in the monsoon?
faqs.a: The short joy rides between Darjeeling and Ghoom usually run through the monsoon, weather permitting. The long services between New Jalpaiguri and Darjeeling are often suspended or cut short when landslides block the line, sometimes for weeks. Check the latest timetable and status with the railway before you travel, and do not plan a tight connection around the train.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Darjeeling in July?
faqs.a: Rarely. In July the mountain is usually behind cloud for days or weeks at a time, though a short clear spell at dawn does happen now and then. If seeing Kanchenjunga is the main reason for your trip, October to December and March to early May give far better chances, with October and November usually the clearest.

faqs.q: Is it safe to travel to the hills during the monsoon?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if you are careful. The main risk is landslides on hill roads, so travel only by day, ideally in the morning, follow your driver's advice about which route is open, and keep a spare day before trains or flights. Avoid long forest treks, riverbeds and North Sikkim in July, and check current status before you travel.
